title: Fulgens and Lucrece
alternative_titles: Fulgens and Lucres
description: Henry Medwall's interlude of the wooing of Lucrece, performed at the household of Cardinal Morton; the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell c. 1512–16.
plot_or_argument: The Roman senator Fulgens promises his daughter Lucrece to the suitor of greater nobility, Publius Cornelius or Gaius Flaminius; the debate on true nobility (virtue versus birth) is interwoven with a subplot in which two serving-men, A and B, woo Lucrece's maid and re-enact the contest in comic parallel. The play breaks off in the unique surviving copy before the conclusion.
narrative_structure: Two-part interlude alternating the serious debate of the senators with the comic subplot of the servants, with direct addresses to the banqueting audience.
principal_characters: Fulgens; Lucrece; Publius Cornelius; Gaius Flaminius; A (servant); B (servant); Joan (Lucrece's maid)
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal and couplets, with prose dialogue in the comic scenes
historical_context: Written for performance at a feast given by Cardinal John Morton (probably Christmas 1497), in whose household Medwall was chaplain; the play adapts Buonaccorso da Montemagno's De vera nobilitate (translated by John Tiptoft c. 1460), and Rastell's printing (c. 1512–16) preserved it for the sixteenth-century stage tradition.
literary_significance: The first surviving secular English play and a landmark in the transition from medieval moral drama to Renaissance comedy; its debate on true nobility and its pairing of serious and comic plots anticipate the structure of Elizabethan drama.
bibliographical_notes: Unique copy (Huntington Library) of Rastell's edition c. 1512–16; modern editions: Fulgens and Lucrece, ed. F. S. Boas and A. W. Reed (1926); The Plays of Henry Medwall, ed. Alan H. Nelson (Brewer, 1980).

title: Nature
alternative_titles: Nature, a goodly interlude of Nature
description: Henry Medwall's morality play of the fall and reformation of Man, the earliest surviving full-scale English morality written for a noble household; printed c. 1530–34 by William Rastell.
plot_or_argument: Nature creates Man and sets Reason and Sensuality over him; Man follows Sensuality into the tavern and the arms of Pride, and the seven deadly sins strip him of his goods; Age and Shamefacedness bring him to repentance, and Reason restores him to grace. The play dramatizes the cycle of innocence, sin, and penitential return.
narrative_structure: Two-part morality play with allegorical personifications, alternating processional scenes of the sins with debate between Reason and Sensuality.
principal_characters: Nature; Man; Reason; Sensuality; Pride; World; Age; Shamefacedness; Innocence
historical_context: Written in the late 1490s, probably for Morton's household like Fulgens and Lucrece; it draws on the tradition of The Castle of Perseverance and Everyman while giving new prominence to worldly temptation, and William Rastell's printing (c. 1530–34) secured its influence on the mid-century interludes.
literary_significance: The earliest surviving English morality play composed for a secular household audience and the first full example of the genre after Everyman; it documents the adaptation of the morality tradition to Renaissance taste and anticipates the moral interludes of the 1560s.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Rastell c. 1530–34 (STC 17779); modern edition: The Plays of Henry Medwall, ed. Alan H. Nelson (Brewer, 1980).

title: The Play of the Weather
alternative_titles: The Play of the Wether
A New and a Very Mery Enterlude of All Maner Wethers
description: John Heywood's interlude in which Jupiter receives petitions for every kind of weather and reconciles them all by leaving the weather as it is; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
plot_or_argument: Jupiter, wishing to settle the world's complaints about the weather, summons the estates of the realm: a gentleman wants fair weather for hunting, a merchant wind for his ships, a ranger frost, a water-miller rain, a laundress sun, a boy snow; each pleads his case, and Jupiter's final decree — that the weather shall continue as it has been — demonstrates the impossibility of pleasing all parties and the wisdom of accepting the established order.
narrative_structure: A single continuous action of successive petitions before Jupiter's throne, ending with a report of Jupiter's decree; the comic petitions build a survey of the commonwealth by estates.
principal_characters: Jupiter; Mery Report (the Vice); The Gentleman; The Merchant; The Ranger; The Water-Miller; The Wind-Miller; The Laundress; The Boy
meter_and_prosody: Couplets and doggerel, with prose in Mery Report's asides
historical_context: Printed by William Rastell in 1533, the year of Henry VIII's divorce crisis and the statute in restraint of appeals; the play's debate on sovereignty and the impossibility of pleasing all suitors has been read as a commentary on royal counsel and the conflicts of the Reformation Parliament.
literary_significance: The best known of Heywood's interludes and a classic of early Tudor political satire: its survey of competing interests remains the liveliest dramatic picture of the Tudor commonwealth, and Mery Report is a landmark in the development of the stage Vice.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1533 (STC 13305); modern editions: The Plays of John Heywood, ed. Richard Axton and Peter Happé (Brewer, 1991).

title: A Play of Love
alternative_titles: The Play of Love
description: John Heywood's debate interlude on the pains and pleasures of love, printed by William Rastell in 1534; the first English play devoted wholly to the analysis of courtship.
plot_or_argument: A man loved but not loving pleads his case against a man loving but not loved, each claiming the sharper pain; their debate is referred to a woman neither loving nor loved, who judges between them; the argument moves through the paradoxes of desire to a reconciliation in which the four parties pair off, demonstrating that love's pleasures and pains are inseparable.
narrative_structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Vice 'Neither-lover-nor-loved' as referee and a concluding judgement that resolves the debate into mutual pairing.
principal_characters: Lover Not Loved; Loved Not Loving; Neither Lover Nor Loved; Both Lover and Loved
historical_context: Printed in 1534, the year of the Act of Supremacy; the play belongs to the courtly debate tradition of the early Tudor household, drawing on the amatory casuistry of the medieval demande d'amour and anticipating the love-debates of Elizabethan drama.
literary_significance: The first sustained dramatic treatment of love in English and the purest example of the debate-interlude form; it links medieval love-casuistry to the Renaissance comedy of courtship.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1534 (STC 13303); modern edition: The Plays of John Heywood, ed. Richard Axton and Peter Happé (Brewer, 1991).

title: The Pardoner and the Friar
alternative_titles: The Pardoner and the Frere
description: John Heywood's anti-clerical farce of a pardoner and a friar who compete for the offerings of a parish church and come to blows in the pulpit; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
plot_or_argument: A pardoner and a friar each claim the right to preach and collect money in a church; each denounces the other's hypocrisy and greed before the parish priest and his neighbour, until the contest descends into a brawl, the parson attempts to expel them, and both are dragged off toward the secular courts — with the parting promise that the devil will decide between them.
narrative_structure: A single-scene farce of rival harangues escalating into violence, framed by the parson's and neighbour's comments.
principal_characters: The Pardoner; The Friar; The Parson; The Neighbour
historical_context: Written c. 1519–33 in the climate of lay criticism of clerical abuses that preceded the Reformation; the play draws on Chaucer's Pardoner and the long anticlerical tradition of estates satire, and its printing in 1533 coincided with the height of the campaign against church wealth.
literary_significance: The most anticlerical of Heywood's plays and a bridge between medieval estates satire and Reformation polemic; it shows the interlude absorbing the controversies of its moment without ceasing to be entertainment.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1533 (STC 13299); modern edition: The Plays of John Heywood, ed. Richard Axton and Peter Happé (Brewer, 1991).

title: The Four PP
alternative_titles: The Play Called the Four PP
The Four Ps
description: John Heywood's best-known farce, a lying contest among a Palmer, a Pardoner, a Pothecary, and a Pedlar; the earliest surviving edition is that of William Middleton, c. 1544.
plot_or_argument: A Palmer, Pardoner, and Pothecary each boast of his trade and its profits, and the Pedlar proposes a contest: whoever tells the greatest lie wins the wager. The Pothecary's tale of a marvellous cure and the Pardoner's account of a soul released from hell's pains — capped by the Palmer's claim that he has met a woman patient and uncomplaining — end the contest, the Palmer winning the palm and the company concluding in good fellowship.
narrative_structure: A single-scene farce built of successive set-piece tales, with the Pedlar as proposer and judge of the wager.
principal_characters: The Palmer; The Pardoner; The Pothecary; The Pedlar
historical_context: Composed c. 1520–30 in Heywood's period as a court entertainer and virginal player to Henry VIII; the lying contest reworks the fabliau tradition (the tale of the patient wife appears in Boccaccio) and the satire of pardons and relics reflects pre-Reformation criticism of popular piety.
literary_significance: The most famous of the Tudor interludes and the classic English stage farce before Shakespeare; its tale of the woman patient in all things circulated into later jest-books and remains the play by which Heywood is chiefly remembered.
bibliographical_notes: Earliest surviving edition c. 1544 (STC 13300), printed by William Middleton; modern editions: The Plays of John Heywood, ed. Richard Axton and Peter Happé (Brewer, 1991).

title: Johan Johan
alternative_titles: A Mery Play between Johan Johan the Husbande, Tyb his Wyfe, and Syr Jhan the Preest
description: John Heywood's one-act farce of a cuckolded husband sent on errands by his wife and her lover the priest; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
plot_or_argument: Johan Johan, suspecting his wife Tyb of entertaining Sir John the priest, is dispatched by her on a series of errands — to mend a pail, to fetch wax — while she dines with the priest; returning to find them feasting on a pie he was sent away from, Johan at last drives the priest out with blows, and the play ends with the husband's triumphant threat to beat Tyb too.
narrative_structure: A single-scene farce of errands and discovery, ending in a cudgel-fight; the play is a dramatization of the anti-clerical fabliau of the priest, the wife, and the credulous husband.
principal_characters: Johan Johan; Tyb (his wife); Sir John (the priest)
historical_context: Printed in 1533 by Rastell, the year that saw the first parliamentary attacks on clerical marriage jurisdiction and mortuary fees; the play's satire of the lecherous parish priest draws on the fabliau tradition of Chaucer's Miller's Tale and the popular anticlerical jest.
literary_significance: The first English farce on the theme of the cuckolded husband and the anticlerical triangle that would recur through the century; its rapid domestic action makes it the most theatrically economical of Heywood's plays.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1533 (STC 13298); modern edition: The Plays of John Heywood, ed. Richard Axton and Peter Happé (Brewer, 1991).

title: Witty and Witless
alternative_titles: A Dialogue on Wit and Folly
description: John Heywood's debate dialogue on the relative happiness of the witty man and the witless, surviving in a single manuscript; first printed in 1846 by the Percy Society.
plot_or_argument: James and John dispute whether it is better to be witty or witless: James argues that wit brings care and envy, John that witlessness is mere animal contentment; each supports his case with proverbs, exempla, and the testimony of fools, until the conclusion grants each condition its proper happiness.
narrative_structure: A continuous debate in alternating speeches, without action, in the manner of the scholastic disputation turned to moral entertainment.
principal_characters: James; John
historical_context: Written c. 1525–33, probably for a household audience; the debate on wit and folly belongs to the Erasmian praise-of-folly tradition, and the play's proverb lore links it to Heywood's collection of proverbs and epigrams.
literary_significance: A minor but revealing document of the Erasmian debate on wisdom and folly in the English household; its survival in manuscript shows the interlude circulating beyond print.
attribution_notes: The manuscript ascribes the work to John Heywood; the attribution is accepted in modern scholarship.
bibliographical_notes: Unique manuscript (British Library, Harley MS 367); first printed by the Percy Society (1846); modern edition: The Plays of John Heywood, ed. Richard Axton and Peter Happé (Brewer, 1991).

title: Wit and Science
alternative_titles: The Play of Wit and Science
description: John Redford's morality play of the courtship of Wit and Science, the masterpiece of the educational interludes written for the choirboys of St Paul's; surviving in a single manuscript and first printed in 1848.
plot_or_argument: Wit, son of Nature, sets out to win the lady Science, daughter of Reason; beguiled by Idleness he falls asleep and is transformed by the enchantment of Ignorance into the fool Ingenio; Shame and Reason restore him, Instruction and Study arm him anew, and he defeats the giant Tediousness, winning Science in a dance of reconciliation. The play celebrates the humanist programme of learning through labour.
narrative_structure: A two-part morality play of quest, fall, and restoration, with songs, dances, and stage spectacle; the action alternates between Wit's education and the comic threats of Tediousness and Idleness.
principal_characters: Wit; Science; Reason; Nature; Idleness; Ignorance; Shame; Instruction; Study; Diligence; Tediousness; Honest Recreation
historical_context: Composed c. 1530–47 by Redford, choirmaster of St Paul's, for performance by the cathedral choirboys; the play belongs to the humanist transformation of the morality tradition into a vehicle for the new learning, and its songs survive with music by Redford himself.
literary_significance: The finest of the school interludes and the purest dramatic expression of Tudor humanist pedagogy; its allegory of the arduous courtship of learning shaped the later academic plays and the tradition of the children's companies.
bibliographical_notes: Unique manuscript (British Library, Add. MS 15233); first printed by the Shakespeare Society (1848); standard edition: Wit and Science, in The Moral Play of Wit and Science, ed. Arthur Brown (Malone Society, 1951).

title: Ralph Roister Doister
alternative_titles: Roister Doister
description: Nicholas Udall's five-act comedy of the braggart Ralph Roister Doister, written c. 1552–54 and printed c. 1566–67; generally regarded as the first English comedy.
plot_or_argument: Ralph Roister Doister, a vainglorious suitor encouraged by the parasite Merrygreek, woos Dame Christian Custance, who is betrothed to the merchant Gawin Goodluck; his letters and verses are read to her as insults, and his siege of her house ends in a comic battle with her maids, the braggart routed by a broom; the play closes with the lovers reunited and Roister Doister invited to dinner — folly corrected without malice.
narrative_structure: Five acts modelled on the Roman comedy of Plautus and Terence, with a braggart soldier, a parasite, and a reunion plot; the action is domestic and the verse a rollicking doggerel.
principal_characters: Ralph Roister Doister; Matthew Merrygreek; Dame Christian Custance; Gawin Goodluck; Tristram Trusty; Madge Mumblecrust; Tibet Talkapace; Annot Alyface
meter_and_prosody: Irregular rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with songs
historical_context: Written c. 1552–54, probably for performance by the boys of Westminster School (Udall was headmaster there from 1555, earlier at Eton); drawing on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus and Terence's Eunuchus, it belongs to the academic revival of Roman comedy that would produce Gammer Gurton's Needle and the school drama of the 1560s.
literary_significance: The first English comedy: it transplants the Roman braggart soldier and parasite into a London setting, joins classical form to native farce, and inaugurates the line that runs through Gammer Gurton's Needle to Shakespeare and Jonson.
bibliographical_notes: First printed c. 1566–67 (STC 24508); standard edition: Roister Doister, in Three Sixteenth-Century Comedies, ed. Charles W. Whitworth (New Mermaids, 1984).

title: The Four Elements
alternative_titles: A New Interlude and a Mery, of the Nature of the Four Elements
description: John Rastell's pedagogical interlude on the four elements and the new geography, printed by the author c. 1520; the first English play designed to teach natural science.
plot_or_argument: Humanity, instructed by Nature and Studious Desire, is taught the four elements, the roundness of the earth, and the new-found lands of America; he is then tempted by Sensual Appetite into the tavern, where he wastes his learning in drinking, and the fragment (the play survives incomplete) breaks off with Experience promising his restoration.
narrative_structure: A morality framework used for instruction: a series of lectures on cosmology and geography alternating with scenes of temptation and fall, with songs (including one with music) and a dance.
principal_characters: Nature; Humanity; Studious Desire; Sensual Appetite; Experience; Ignorance; The Taverner
historical_context: Printed c. 1520 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, who had himself attempted a voyage to the New World in 1517; the play's geography lesson celebrates the discovery of America, and its music survives in the unique fragment (British Library).
literary_significance: The first English play to teach science and geography, and a pioneering attempt to harness the stage to the new learning; it documents the arrival of the Age of Discovery in English popular culture.
bibliographical_notes: Unique surviving copy (fragment, British Library, C.39.b.17), printed by Rastell c. 1520 (STC 20722); modern edition: The Four Elements, ed. Roger Coleman (1971), and in Three Rastell Plays, ed. Richard Axton (Brewer, 1979).

title: Gentleness and Nobility
alternative_titles: Of Gentylnes and Nobylyte
description: A debate interlude on the nature of true nobility, printed by John Rastell c. 1529 and attributed to Rastell (or, by some, to John Heywood); an early dramatic statement of the humanist case that virtue, not birth, makes the gentleman.
plot_or_argument: A Knight, a Merchant, and a Ploughman dispute whether gentleness resides in ancestry or in virtue; the Ploughman, arguing that nobility of birth without worth is empty, is supported against the Knight's hereditary claims, and the debate — refereed by the Philosopher — concludes with the definition of true gentleness as virtuous living, with a sharp satire of idle gentlemen who live off others' labour.
narrative_structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Philosopher as moderator and the three estates as speakers; the debate is enlivened by comic abuse between the Knight and the Ploughman.
principal_characters: The Knight; The Merchant; The Ploughman; The Philosopher
historical_context: Printed c. 1529, in the year of the Reformation Parliament; the play's defence of labour and its satire of idle gentry voice the social criticism of the humanist commonwealth tradition (More's Utopia, Starkey's Dialogue), and its attribution to Rastell connects it to the More circle.
literary_significance: The first English play devoted wholly to the question of true nobility, and a rare dramatic voice for the commonwealth critique of hereditary privilege; it anticipates the social debates of Elizabethan drama.
attribution_notes: Printed without author's name; the play is traditionally attributed to John Rastell (whose press produced it), with John Heywood also proposed; modern scholarship accepts Rastell as the likeliest author without certainty.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1529 (STC 20723, fragmentary unique copy); modern edition: Three Rastell Plays, ed. Richard Axton (Brewer, 1979).

title: Gammer Gurton's Needle
alternative_titles: A Ryght Pithy, Pleasaunt and Merie Comedie: Intytuled Gammer Gurtons Nedle
description: The classic English village farce of the lost needle, composed c. 1552–53, probably at Christ's College, Cambridge, and printed in 1575; the second of the two earliest English comedies (with Ralph Roister Doister).
plot_or_argument: Gammer Gurton's precious needle is lost while mending the breeches of her servant Hodge; the whole household turns out to search, suspicion falls on the neighbour Dame Chat, and the village curate Doctor Rat is beaten in a confusion of break-ins and brawls; the needle is at last discovered — in the seat of Hodge's breeches — with a resounding yell, and the company shares the ale in reconciliation.
narrative_structure: Five acts in a single village setting, modelled on Roman comedy but filled with native farce: the plot turns on the lost object, the false accusation, and the comic discovery.
principal_characters: Gammer Gurton; Hodge; Diccon the Bedlam; Dame Chat; Doctor Rat; Master Bayly; Tib; Cock
meter_and_prosody: Rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with the famous drinking song 'Back and side go bare'
historical_context: Composed c. 1552–53, with the title-page attribution of the 1575 edition to 'Mr. S. Master of Art' generally identified as William Stevenson of Christ's College, Cambridge, where the play was probably acted; it belongs to the university revival of classical comedy in the 1550s.
literary_significance: One of the two founding comedies of the English stage: its picture of village life, its rich dialect comedy, and its plot of the lost needle set the pattern for English farce from Shakespeare's Merry Wives to the twentieth century.
attribution_notes: The 1575 title page ascribes the play to 'Mr. S. Master of Art', identified by modern scholarship (most fully by Charles W. Whitworth) as William Stevenson of Christ's College, Cambridge; the attribution is probable rather than certain.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1575 (STC 23263); standard edition: Gammer Gurton's Needle, in Three Sixteenth-Century Comedies, ed. Charles W. Whitworth (New Mermaids, 1984).

title: Respublica
alternative_titles: A Merry Interlude Entitled Respublica
description: An anonymous Protestant morality play of the commonwealth, written for performance at Christmas 1553 during the first months of Mary I's reign; a sophisticated political allegory of the misgovernment of the 1540s.
plot_or_argument: Respublica, the widowed commonwealth, is robbed by Avarice and his crew — Oppression, Adulation, and Insolence (disguised as Policy, Honesty, and Authority) — who plunder her goods and divide them among themselves; the four sisters People, Verity, Peace, and Justice return, strip the thieves of their disguises, and restore the commonwealth, with Mercy pronouncing judgement and the audience promised amendment under the new queen.
narrative_structure: Five acts of morality allegory applied to contemporary politics, with the Vice Avarice doubling his disguises and a final scene of restoration and loyal address to Mary I.
principal_characters: Respublica; Avarice; Adulation; Oppression; Insolence; People; Verity; Peace; Justice; Mercy; Nemesis
historical_context: Performed at Christmas 1553, evidently by a company of boys, in the first months of Mary's reign; the play's allegory of the plunder of the commonwealth under Edward VI's ministers (Somerset and Northumberland) and its restoration under the Catholic queen marks a rare moment when the morality tradition served immediate dynastic politics.
literary_significance: The most politically sophisticated of the sixteenth-century moralities: its allegory of the commonwealth, its disguised Vices, and its address to the monarch anticipate the political drama of the Elizabethan stage, and it documents the mid-Tudor crisis of counsel and plunder.
attribution_notes: No author is named in the manuscript; Nicholas Udall has been proposed by some scholars, but the attribution remains unproven, and the work is treated as anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Unique manuscript (British Library, Add. MS 15233), first printed by the Early English Text Society in 1869 (ed. Leonard A. Magnus, EETS e.s. 94); standard edition: Respublica: An Interlude for Christmas 1553, ed. W. W. Greg (EETS o.s. 226, 1952).

title: Godly Queen Hester
alternative_titles: A New Interlude Drawn out of the Holy Scripture of Godly Queen Hester
description: An anonymous interlude on the biblical story of Esther, printed in 1561 but composed c. 1525–29; a political allegory in which the virtuous queen and her wise counsellor save the realm from the wicked minister.
plot_or_argument: King Ahasuerus, misled by the proud Aman, signs a decree against the Jews; Queen Hester, advised by the wise Mardocheus, intercedes with the king at the risk of her life, exposes Aman's malice, and obtains his overthrow and the deliverance of her people — with the collop-eating scene of Aman's gluttony played as comic Vice-business.
narrative_structure: A continuous interlude alternating the counsel scenes of Hester and Mardocheus with the comic scenes of Aman and his servants, ending in judgement and the elevation of Mardocheus.
principal_characters: King Ahasuerus; Queen Hester; Mardocheus; Aman; Ardion (Aman's servant); Hardydardy; Pride; Adulation; Ambition
historical_context: Composed c. 1525–29, almost certainly for a noble household: the story of Esther had long served as an allegory of good counsel and royal deliverance, and the play has been read (by Greg Walker and others) as a veiled commentary on the fall of Wolsey, in which the virtuous queen intercedes against an overmighty minister.
literary_significance: The first surviving English dramatization of the Esther story and a striking example of the interlude as political counsel; it shows biblical drama absorbing the new humanist debate on counsel and tyranny.
bibliographical_notes: Unique copy of the 1561 edition (STC 13251); standard edition: Godly Queen Hester, ed. W. W. Greg (Materialien zur Kunde des älteren Englischen Dramas 5, 1904).

title: Jacob and Esau
alternative_titles: A New Mery and Wittie Comedie or Enterlude, Newely Imprinted, Treating upon the Historie of Jacob and Esau
description: An anonymous Protestant biblical interlude on the story of Jacob and Esau from Genesis, printed in 1568; one of the liveliest mid-century dramatizations of the doctrine of election.
plot_or_argument: The play follows Genesis 25–27: the differing natures of the twins Jacob and Esau, the sale of the birthright for a pottage, Isaac's blessing of Jacob obtained through Rebecca's counsel, and Esau's rage and reconciliation; the serious matter of election is framed by the comic servants of the household (Ragan, Mido, and the boy Abra) whose tricks and misadventures mirror the plot.
narrative_structure: Five acts with act and scene divisions, alternating the biblical action with a fully developed comic subplot, and a prologue arguing that election is the play's theme.
principal_characters: Isaac; Rebecca; Jacob; Esau; Ragan; Mido; Abra; Deborah; Hanan
historical_context: Composed c. 1550–58 in the Edwardian and Marian years, when the doctrine of predestination was at the centre of English religious debate; the play's prologue makes the case for the godly theatre, and it was printed in 1568 for the Elizabethan market.
literary_significance: The most accomplished of the mid-century biblical interludes and an important document of Protestant dramatic theory; its comic subplot anticipates the structure of Elizabethan biblical and history plays.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1568 (STC 14325); standard edition: Jacob and Esau, in The Malone Society Reprints (1956).

title: Nice Wanton
alternative_titles: A Preaty Interlude Called Nice Wanton
description: An anonymous Protestant morality interlude of the divergent fates of three children, printed in 1560; a dramatization of godly education and its neglect.
plot_or_argument: Xantippe's three children grow up under her indulgence: Ishmael and Dalila fall into idleness, gambling, and prostitution, and come to the gallows; the godly Barnabas, who studies scripture, is spared and comforts his repentant mother and sister; the Vice Iniquity frames the action, and the epilogue draws the moral of education and the rod.
narrative_structure: A continuous morality play of two contrasted life-paths, with Iniquity as the linking Vice, songs, and a concluding moral address.
principal_characters: Xantippe; Barnabas; Ishmael; Dalila; Iniquity; Eulalia; The Worldly Shame
historical_context: Composed c. 1547–53, in the years of the Edwardian Reformation, when the godly education of children became a central Protestant theme; printed in 1560 for the Elizabethan market, with a title-page woodcut of the flogging schoolmaster.
literary_significance: A representative Protestant morality whose twin plots of the saved and the damned child dramatize the educational programme of the Reformation; it marks the absorption of humanist pedagogy into the morality tradition.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1560 (STC 25016); modern editions: Nice Wanton, ed. Leonard Tennenhouse, in Renaissance Drama n.s. 15 (1984); also in Specimens of the Pre-Shaksperean Drama, ed. J. M. Manly (1897).

title: Lusty Juventus
alternative_titles: An Interlude Called Lusty Juventus
description: A Protestant morality interlude of the youth Juventus, tempted by Hypocrisy and the devil but restored by Good Counsel and God's Merciful Promises; printed c. 1550 with the author's name given as R. Wever.
plot_or_argument: Juventus (Youth), fresh from his conversion, is tempted by the devil's instruments — Hypocrisy, Fellowship, and Abominable Living — who draw him into sin and despair; Good Counsel and Knowledge recall him, God's Merciful Promises assures him of forgiveness through Christ, and the play ends with Juventus's restoration and a call to the audience to follow his example.
narrative_structure: A continuous morality play of temptation, fall, and restoration, with the devil and Hypocrisy as the comic Vices and a concluding address to the young.
principal_characters: Juventus; Good Counsel; Knowledge; God's Merciful Promises; The Devil; Hypocrisy; Fellowship; Abominable Living
historical_context: Composed in the early years of the Edwardian Reformation (c. 1547–53) and printed c. 1550; its polemic against hypocrisy and works-righteousness and its emphasis on justification by faith make it a direct dramatic expression of Protestant doctrine for a young audience.
literary_significance: The most explicitly doctrinal of the Edwardian moralities and a prime example of the interlude as Reformation propaganda; its title character became the proverbial type of the reformed youth.
attribution_notes: The title page names 'R. Wever' as author; nothing further is known of him, and the ascription cannot be independently confirmed.
bibliographical_notes: First printed c. 1550 (STC 25148); modern edition: Lusty Juventus, in Specimens of the Pre-Shaksperean Drama, ed. J. M. Manly (1897); also ed. J. S. Farmer (Tudor Facsimile Texts, 1907).

title: Calisto and Melebea
alternative_titles: A New Comedy in English in Manner of an Interlude
description: An anonymous English adaptation of the first four acts of Fernando de Rojas's Celestina, printed by John Rastell c. 1525–30; the first English version of the Spanish classic.
plot_or_argument: Calisto, rejected by Melibea, seeks the help of the old bawd Celestina, who wins the lady for him by her arts; the fragment (the play survives incomplete) follows the first movement of Rojas's tragicomedy through the lovers' meeting, ending before the deaths that close the original.
narrative_structure: A scene-by-scene dramatization of the opening of the Celestina, compressed into interlude form, with the bawd's character preserved in translation.
principal_characters: Calisto; Melibea; Celestina; Sempronio; Parmeno
historical_context: Printed c. 1525–30, probably by John Rastell, whose press had connections to the Spanish trade through the More circle (More's daughter married into the Rastell family, and Vives was in England); the Celestina, the great Spanish masterpiece of 1499, was thus introduced to English readers a generation before Mabbe's full translation.
literary_significance: The first English adaptation of the Celestina and an early witness to Anglo-Spanish literary exchange; it extends the range of the interlude to tragicomic romance and anticipates the Elizabethan stage's use of continental fiction.
attribution_notes: No author is named; the play has been attributed to John Rastell on the evidence of the press and the More circle's Spanish connections, but the attribution is conjectural.
bibliographical_notes: Unique fragment (Bodleian Library) of the edition c. 1525–30 (STC 20721); modern edition: An Enterlude of Calisto and Melebea, in the Malone Society Reprints (1908).

title: Hickscorner
alternative_titles: Hycke Scorner
description: An anonymous early morality interlude of the conversion of three rogues — Freewill, Imagination, and the Vice Hickscorner — printed by Wynkyn de Worde c. 1513–15.
plot_or_argument: Freewill and Imagination, fallen into idleness and vice, meet the hardened rogue Hickscorner, who boasts of his crimes and rails at virtue; Pity and Contemplation reprove them, and the three rogues are brought to repentance, confess their sins, and set out on pilgrimage, with the play ending in a vision of the joys of heaven.
narrative_structure: A continuous morality play in two movements — the rogues' boasting fellowship and their conversion — with the Vice Hickscorner as the play's comic engine.
principal_characters: Freewill; Imagination; Hickscorner; Pity; Contemplation; Perseverance
historical_context: Printed c. 1513–15 by Wynkyn de Worde, in the generation after Everyman; the play's tavern scenes and rogue-cant document the underworld of early Tudor London, and its popularity carried it through editions to the 1560s.
literary_significance: One of the earliest printed English moralities and the first to centre on the conversion of rogues; its Vice, Hickscorner, is a landmark in the development of the stage devil's comic heir, and its tavern realism anticipates the rogue literature of the Elizabethans.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1513–15 (STC 14039, unique copy, British Library); modern edition: Hickscorner, in The Malone Society Reprints (1908), ed. W. W. Greg; also in Specimens of the Pre-Shaksperean Drama, ed. J. M. Manly (1897).

title: Interlude of Youth
alternative_titles: The Enterlude of Youth
description: An anonymous morality interlude of the fall and repentance of Youth, composed c. 1513–14 and printed c. 1530–35; a compact dramatization of the prodigal's return.
plot_or_argument: Youth, flattered by Riot, Pride, and Lechery, abandons Charity and Humility for the tavern and the stews; Charity and Humility lament and warn him, and Youth, brought low, repents and returns to virtue, ending with a prayer for the king and the audience's amendment.
narrative_structure: A short two-part morality play of temptation and return, with the Vices' songs and taunts alternating with Charity's warnings.
principal_characters: Youth; Charity; Humility; Riot; Pride; Lechery
historical_context: Composed c. 1513–14, probably for a noble household (the prayer for the king suggests courtly performance), and printed c. 1530–35; it belongs to the same early Tudor wave as Hickscorner and Magnificence, in which the morality play becomes a vehicle for aristocratic moral counsel.
literary_significance: A compact and influential example of the early Tudor morality, dramatizing the prodigal theme that would run through the century to the Elizabethan stage; it survives as a witness to the interlude's household origins.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1530–35 (STC 14111a, unique imperfect copy, Lambeth Palace Library); modern edition: The Enterlude of Youth, in The Malone Society Reprints (1905).
